paper.citation: Kowal I, Donohue B, Barchard KA, Kraus SW, Allen DN. Examination of the Impact of Substance Use on Sport Training and Competition in Collegiate Athletes. Sport Social Work Journal. 2025 (advance online publication).
paper.abstract: A four-item measure of how alcohol and illicit drug use interfere with sport performance in training and competition was psychometrically evaluated in 285 collegiate athletes from NCAA, club and intramural teams. The measure showed good one-week test-retest reliability, was positively related to psychiatric symptoms and to substance use frequency, and was higher in male athletes.
paper.tldr: A short self-report measure of how alcohol and drug use interfere with training and competition showed good one-week reliability and modest links to psychiatric symptoms and substance use in collegiate athletes. It may help staff gauge the sport impact of substance use, but it is not a diagnostic tool.
paper.methods: Cross-sectional psychometric study at one Division 1 university in which 285 athletes completed the four-item interference measure, the SCL-90-R, and a Timeline Follow-Back substance use measure, and a structured clinical interview for substance use disorder was administered. A subsample of 74 participants who reported substance use and interest in intervention completed a second battery one week later, and the authors compared scores by diagnosis, gender, ethnicity, year in school and athlete type.
paper.findings: One-week test-retest reliability was good (ICC = 0.74). Scores correlated with psychiatric symptoms (r = .217, n = 280, controlling for age, gender and athlete type) and with 30-day substance use frequency (r = .255, n = 74). Male athletes scored higher, scores did not differ by ethnicity or year in school, and NCAA athletes scored lower than club and intramural athletes. Athletes with a current substance use disorder scored higher only as a non-significant trend (p = .08).
paper.limitations: The second-phase sample was small (n = 74), and those participants were required to pursue psychological programming, which limits generalisability. Marginalised groups were not explicitly recruited, and the authors note a larger sample would have given more power to test the diagnostic comparison. All participants came from one university.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff working with collegiate athletes could use the four sport-interference items as a starting point for conversations about how substance use affects training and competition. Because the study did not establish that the measure identifies substance use disorder, a concerning response should prompt clinical assessment rather than a diagnosis.
paper.athleteDev: Performance staff can use this four-item measure as a brief, sport-specific way to ask how alcohol or drug use affects training and competition in collegiate athletes. Scores reflect athletes' self-reported interference and do not measure performance itself.
paper.rtp: The study did not include injured athletes or return-to-sport decisions, so it cannot be used to guide return to sport or medical clearance.
